prerequisites: Students must master specific mathematical and physical knowledge (Statics). It is recommended not to enroll without having successfully completed the subjects where these are taught.

learning_outcomes.text: Provide tools to understand and identify the types of stresses that can occur in construction, structural, or mechanical elements, assess the stresses and deformations they can reach, and begin to comparatively weigh the values obtained from these calculations against limit values established by proven prior experience (relevant regulations) or acquired practically, so that they can define constructive sections and predetermine the internal equilibrium conditions that the materials will withstand.
Analyze the state of stresses and deformations at a point in a continuous medium.
Know and apply the relationships between stresses and deformations of a solid.
Characterize the load states and types of forces in mechanical prisms.
Apply methods for analyzing the stresses and deformations generated by load states.
Apply tools to dimension different simple elements such as beams, supports, cables, shafts, etc., for strength and rigidity.
Understanding and interpretation of texts and data, development of skills for their concretization and clear and concise exposition.
Aptitude for the distribution of resources and time and their implementation in real situations.
Ability to use scientific-technical tools for solving calculation and design problems in Industrial Engineering and aptitude for finding sustainable engineering solutions.
Ability for teamwork and capacity for the development of multidisciplinary projects.
Knowledge and use of the principles of strength of materials.

syllabus_topics: INTRODUCTION TO STRENGTH OF MATERIALS: Strength of materials. Load states. Types of efforts. Hypotheses in S. of M. Types of connection. Technical materials. Calculation methods. Equivalent limit stresses.

TENSION AND COMPRESSION: Intuitive concept of tension and compression. Laws of tension and compression. Deformations occasioned by tension and compression forces. Variable loads. Solids of equal tensile (compressive) strength. Statically indeterminate problems in tension and compression. Thin rings. Stress concentration. Transverse deformation. Strain energy in tension-compression. Applications of the concept of strain energy.
SHEAR: Definition. Shear stress. Deformations. Other shear stresses. Biaxial tension and compression. Shear strain energy. Connecting elements. Shear calculation of bolted joints. Welded joints.

TORSION: Torsion moment. Torsion of a straight-axis bar with a flat circular normal section. Deformations in torsion. Observations on torsion. Torsion springs. Torsion in thin-walled tubes. Torsional strain energy. Torsion of solid rectangular section bars. Torsion of any type of section.

BENDING: Definitions. Equilibrium conditions in a section. Equilibrium stresses in a section under simple bending. Shear stress on a section of a system subjected to bending. Solids of equal bending strength. Graphical representation of bending moments and shear forces. Sign convention. Torsion center. Elastic deformation of a material system due to bending. Tangent to the elastic line at a point. Application of the moment law for calculating deformations. Transverse deformation. Mohr's theorems. Bending strain energy. Castigliano's theorem. Mohr-Castigliano method for calculating deformations. Universal equation method. Conjugate beam method.
Practice: Calculation examples after theoretical exposition.
Practice: Problems or assignments for individual completion and subsequent correction in class or seminars.
teaching_methods: Practical classes (solving exercises on the board with student participation)
Problem solving/assignments for individual completion and correction in class or seminars

assessment_methods.method: Continuous assessment (including collected exercises, practical exercises, and attendance)

assessment_rules: The continuous assessment score will be 35% of the final grade, with collected exercises having more specific weight (x1) than exercises solved in practical hours (x0.3 to x0.7) and attendance (x0.1). The final exam consists of four exercises totaling 10 points, and the student must obtain 5 out of 10 points to pass the course. The final exam's score is weighted at 65% of the final grade. The continuous assessment grade may be considered for the resit exam, exceptionally, if the student informs within the first four weeks of the course, and part of the continuous assessment can be compensated with exercises and tutorial follow-up.
